title: Graphic Design Basics
summary: Learn the core ideas behind clear, attractive design: layout, hierarchy, colour, type and images, then make a poster, social post and logo idea with free phone apps.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No design experience or special software needed; a phone or tablet is enough

body.p: Good design is not decoration. A designer makes something so that a particular person can understand it quickly and do something. Before you open any app, answer two questions: what is this for, and who is it for? Everything else, from colour to font to picture, is chosen to serve those two answers.

Every design should have one main job. A poster for a school debate must make people notice the date, time and place. A social post for a bakery in Accra should make people want to order. A sign on a clinic door must tell people which way to go. If you try to make a design do five jobs, it does none of them well. Write the job in one sentence first, for example: Get Year 10 students in Freetown to attend the careers fair on Friday.

body.h: Audience: who will see it, and where

list: Age and language: a poster for primary pupils needs bigger, simpler words than one for university students. Use the language your audience actually reads.
Setting: a poster read from across a corridor needs large text; a phone post is read at arm's length in a few seconds.
Culture: colours and symbols carry different meanings in different places, so check with people from your community rather than assuming.
Device: many of your viewers will see your work on a small phone screen with the sun shining on it. Design for that.

body.p: Hierarchy means arranging things so the eye knows what to read first, second and third. Without it, everything shouts equally and the viewer gives up. You create hierarchy mainly with size, weight (thin to bold), colour and position. The biggest, boldest, highest-contrast item is read first.

Worked example: a fundraising car-wash flyer for a youth club in Nairobi. Level one is the headline: CAR WASH FOR CHARITY, large and bold. Level two is the key facts: Saturday, 9 am to 2 pm, Kenyatta Road, in medium size. Level three is the small print: price per car and a contact number, in the smallest readable size. A viewer who glances for two seconds still gets the main message.

body.tip: The squint test: blur your eyes or step back from the screen. The one or two things you can still see are your real top level. If they are not the most important things, change the sizes.

body.p: A simple way to plan hierarchy is to rank your content before designing. Write the text items in a list and number them 1, 2, 3. Item 1 gets the largest size, and each lower number gets less emphasis.

Layout is where things sit on the page. A famous set of four simple rules, often remembered as CRAP, helps beginners make a tidy layout: Contrast, Repetition, Alignment and Proximity. The name is a memory trick, and the rules are useful on any app or paper.

Contrast means making different things look clearly different. If two items are meant to be different, such as a headline and body text, make the difference big enough that nobody thinks it was an accident. Contrast comes from size, weight, colour, and light versus dark. Weak contrast, such as two nearly equal sizes of text, looks like a mistake.

Repetition means reusing the same style so a design feels connected: the same fonts, colours, button shapes or margins on every page or slide. In a school magazine, if every page number sits in the same corner in the same style, the pages feel like one product. Repetition also builds a brand, because people begin to recognise your look.

Alignment means every item lines up with something else on the page, along an edge or a centre line. Items placed at random look messy even if each one is nice. Choose one main alignment, usually left, and keep to it. Left-aligned text is easiest to read for English and other languages written left to right. Centred text is fine for short headings, but long centred paragraphs are tiring to read.

Proximity means putting related items close together and separating unrelated items. In an invitation, the date, time and place belong together as a group, with extra space before the next group, such as the RSVP phone number. When things are grouped well, the viewer understands the structure without reading a word.

list: Contrast: make different things clearly different.
Repetition: reuse the same styles for a consistent look.
Alignment: line things up on shared edges.
Proximity: group related items and separate the rest.

body.p: White space, also called negative space, is the empty area around things. It is not wasted. It gives the eye a place to rest and makes the important parts stand out. Beginners often fill every corner. Try instead to keep a margin of the same size on all sides, and leave a clear gap between groups. If a design feels crowded, remove something before you shrink everything.

body.tip: Many design apps let you turn on guides or a grid. Use them to snap your items to the same edges. It is the fastest way to get clean alignment on a phone, where fingers are less precise than a mouse.

lessons.title: Colour: hue, saturation, brightness and readability

body.p: Colour grabs attention and sets a mood, but it is also the most common reason text becomes hard to read. This lesson gives you a vocabulary and one rule you can check with numbers.

list: Hue is the basic colour family: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.
Saturation is how pure or intense the colour is. High saturation is vivid; low saturation looks greyer and calmer.
Brightness (also called lightness or value) is how light or dark the colour is, from black to white.

body.p: Most design apps show these as sliders or a colour wheel. Hue is the position on the wheel, saturation is the distance from the grey centre, and brightness is the light-to-dark slider. Changing only brightness gives you a family of matching shades, such as light green, green and dark green, which always look good together.

list: One colour plus neutrals: pick one hue, then use white, black and grey. Very safe and professional.
Analogous: colours next to each other on the wheel, such as blue and green. Calm and harmonious.
Complementary: colours opposite each other on the wheel, such as blue and orange. Energetic; use one as the main colour and the other in small amounts.

body.p: A good habit is the 60-30-10 idea: about 60 percent a main colour, 30 percent a second colour and 10 percent an accent for the most important button or word. It is a guide, not a law.

Text must stand out from its background. Accessibility guidelines called WCAG measure this with a contrast ratio from 1:1 (no difference) to 21:1 (black on white). They ask for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and at least 3:1 for large text. Many free contrast checker tools online let you type two colours and read the ratio.

body.code:
Black on white             21 : 1   excellent
Dark blue 0B3D91 on white  10.0 : 1  very good
White on dark green 1B5E20 7.9 : 1  very good
Grey 767676 on white       4.5 : 1   just passes
Light grey AAAAAA on white 2.3 : 1   fails
White on orange FF9800     2.2 : 1   fails
Yellow on white            1.1 : 1   almost invisible

body.p: These ratios are calculated from the standard formula. Notice that pale grey text and yellow on white fail badly, even though they look pretty on a bright screen. Outdoors, in sunlight, low-contrast text vanishes. Always test by looking at your design on a phone with the brightness turned down.

Roughly one in twelve men and a smaller number of women have some form of colour-vision difference, with red and green confusion being the most common. Never use red versus green alone to carry meaning, such as in a chart or a pass/fail label. Add a second signal: a word, a pattern, an icon, or a clear difference in lightness. Dark blue and orange are usually easy to tell apart. A useful test is to convert your design to greyscale: if you can still tell the parts apart, it works for most people.

body.tip: Choose meaning with care: red often means stop or danger and green often means go, but not in every culture or situation. Always label the meaning in words as well.

body.p: Typography is the art of arranging text so that it is both readable and expressive. Most designs are mostly text, so small typography choices make a large difference. Pick fewer fonts, use them well, and test on a small screen.

list: Serif fonts have small strokes on the ends of letters. They often feel traditional and are common in books and newspapers.
Sans-serif fonts have clean ends with no strokes. They are common on screens and feel modern and simple.
Display or decorative fonts are fancy, such as handwriting styles. Use them only for a few large words, never for paragraphs.
Monospace fonts give every letter the same width. They are used for computer code.

body.p: Use at most two fonts in one design, and often one font family in different weights is enough. A reliable pairing is a bold font for headings with a simple, calm font for body text. Choose fonts that are clearly different from each other, such as a serif heading with a sans-serif body. Two fonts that are almost the same look like a mistake. Keep the pairing the same across your whole project, which is repetition from the last lesson.

On a phone, body text should be comfortable to read at arm's length. In a social post, a common guide is to keep the main message short and large, and avoid any text so small you must pinch to read it. For printed posters, headlines need to be read from a distance, so make them very large. Line spacing, called leading, matters too: a line height of about 1.4 to 1.6 times the text size is comfortable for paragraphs, while tight spacing is fine for big headlines.

list: Line length: aim for roughly 40 to 70 characters per line on a page; short lines on a phone are normal.
Keep paragraphs short and leave blank space between them.
Use bold for emphasis, and avoid underlining, which looks like a link on screens.
Avoid ALL CAPITALS for long text. Capitals are slower to read; save them for a short heading.
Letter spacing: widen it slightly for small capital headings, but leave it normal for body text.

body.p: Worked example: the poster for a debate. Heading: a bold sans-serif at 72 points. Details: the same family in regular weight at 28 points. Small print: 18 points. Three sizes, one font family, and the hierarchy is clear. Compare that with five different fonts in five sizes, which would look noisy and amateur.

body.tip: Check text against its background, including over photos. If words sit on a busy image, add a solid or semi-transparent shape behind the text, or darken the picture slightly, until the text is easy to read.

body.p: Pictures can make a design memorable, but a blurry photo ruins it. To avoid problems you need to understand pixels and the common file formats.

A photo is a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels. A photo that is 1200 pixels wide by 800 pixels tall has 1200 x 800 = 960,000 pixels. If you stretch a small image to fill a large space, the pixels get bigger and the picture looks blurry or blocky. Resolution is how many pixels you have for the size you need. Always start with a picture that is at least as large as the space you want to fill, and never enlarge a small photo much.

For printing, a common target is 300 pixels per inch (ppi). An A4 sheet is about 8.27 by 11.69 inches, so a full-page A4 print at 300 ppi needs roughly 2480 x 3508 pixels. For a screen or phone, you need far fewer pixels. Many social apps suggest sizes about 1080 pixels wide, but sizes change over time, so check the current guidance inside the app you use.

list: Raster images (photos, PNG, JPG) are made of pixels. They get blurry when enlarged.
Vector images (SVG, and many logos) are made of mathematical shapes. They stay sharp at any size, from a phone icon to a billboard.

body.p: A logo is best made as a vector so it can be printed on a small badge or a large banner without losing quality. Many free design apps can export an SVG, and you can usually check by zooming in a lot. Edges that stay clean are vector.

body.code:
PNG   Pixels, no quality loss, supports transparent background.
      Best for: logos, text, screenshots, graphics with flat colour.
JPG   Pixels, smaller file because of compression that loses some detail.
      Best for: photographs and sharing quickly on slow data.
PDF   A document that keeps layout, fonts and images together.
      Best for: printing, posters and sending a finished document.
SVG   Vector shapes that scale without blur.
      Best for: logos and icons for websites and print.

body.p: Worked example: you design a logo for a youth football club in Lusaka. Export a PNG with a transparent background to place on photos, export an SVG so a printer can make a large banner, and keep the original project file so you can edit later. For a photo-heavy flyer to send on WhatsApp, a JPG keeps the file small and uses less mobile data. For a print shop, a PDF is usually the safest.

body.tip: Save a copy of your editable project before exporting. A PNG or JPG cannot be turned back into separate layers, so you could not change the text later.

body.p: Also remember that each time you save a JPG again, a little more detail is lost. Keep your original photo and export from the project each time.

Time to practise. These projects work in any free design app on a phone or tablet, because the steps do not depend on a particular tool. Apps change their menus often, so look for the same ideas under whatever names your app uses: new design with custom size, text, shapes, images, layers, align, and export or share.

steps: Write the job in one sentence: who is the event for and what should they do? Example: Invite Year 9 students to the inter-house quiz on Thursday.
List the content in order of importance: event name, date and time, place, one line of detail, contact.
Create a portrait page. Choose A4 or A3 if you will print it, and set a margin around the edge.
Pick a background colour, then place the title in the largest, boldest style. Check contrast of text on the background.
Add the date, time and place together as one group, with space before the contact line.
Add one picture or shape for interest. Keep it simple.
Squint test, then view at phone size. Fix anything you cannot read.
Export as PDF for printing and PNG or JPG for sharing.
Decide the single message, such as: New student discount this week.
Create a square or portrait design at the size the app recommends.
Put a short headline in large text, with at most about eight words.
Use your brand colours and one or two fonts, the same as your previous posts, for repetition.
Keep important text away from the edges so it is not cropped by the app.
Zoom out to check it is readable at thumbnail size on a phone.
Export as PNG for sharp text, or JPG if the post has a photo and you need a smaller file.

body.p: A logo should be simple, distinct and work in one colour. Try this process for a made-up business, such as a tailor in Kumasi called Sewing Star.

steps: Write three words that describe the business: neat, friendly, modern.
Sketch ten quick ideas on paper. Do not judge them yet.
Pick the best two and recreate them with basic shapes in your app. A needle, a star or the first letter work well.
Choose one colour plus black or white. Check it on both a white and a dark background.
Test it very small, like a phone icon, and very large. Remove details that disappear when small.
Place the name next to the symbol in one clean font.
Export as SVG and as a transparent PNG.

body.tip: Show your design to two other people for five seconds and ask what they remember. If they miss the main message, your hierarchy needs work.

body.p: Designers constantly use pictures, fonts, icons and music. Taking other people's work without permission is unfair to the creator and can lead to legal problems. The rules differ from country to country, but a few ideas are shared in the places Ace learners live, and the safest habit is simple: only use work you made yourself or work you have clear permission to use.

Copyright is the right that automatically belongs to the creator of a photo, drawing, text, music or design. The creator does not have to register it or add a sign. A picture found with a web search is usually not free to use just because it appeared online. Credit alone does not equal permission either: writing "photo from Google" is not a licence.

A licence is the creator's written permission, with conditions. Free image libraries and design apps state their conditions on each image or in their terms. Always read what is allowed, especially if you will use the design to earn money.

list: Public domain or CC0: the creator gives up the rights, so you can use it freely, with no credit required.
Creative Commons CC BY: you may use it if you give credit to the creator.
CC BY-SA: credit is needed, and your new work must be shared with the same licence.
CC BY-NC: credit needed, and not for commercial use, so it is not suitable for a paid business job.
Royalty-free: you pay once or use for free under the licence terms, but it is not always free of restrictions.

body.p: Fonts are software and have licences too. Fonts that come with your design app are usually fine for projects made in that app, but check the terms for commercial use. Do not copy another organisation's logo or imitate a real bank, school or government office, because that can mislead people and may be illegal.

list: Prefer your own photos, drawings and icons.
Use images from libraries that clearly state they are free to use, and read the conditions.
Write the credit in the format the creator asks for: title, creator, source and licence.
Get permission before posting a photo of a recognisable person, and be extra careful with pictures of children.
Keep a note of where each asset came from, so you can prove permission later.

body.tip: If you are not sure whether you can use something, do not use it. Make your own, or ask the creator for permission in writing.

quiz.q: A designer makes a flyer where the date, time and place are spread to three different corners, with the phone number in the middle. Which principle is mainly broken?
options: Proximity, because related information is not grouped together
Repetition, because the same colour appears twice on the page
Contrast, because the page background is white and plain
Hierarchy, because the flyer has a heading at the top

quiz.q: You must choose a text colour for a white poster. Which gives the most readable normal-size text?
options: Light grey AAAAAA, about 2.3 to 1 contrast
Dark blue 0B3D91, about 10 to 1 contrast
Pale yellow FFEB3B, about 1.2 to 1 contrast
Orange FF9800, about 2.2 to 1 contrast on white
Which colour family it belongs to, such as red or blue
How light or dark it is, from near white to near black
How pure and intense a colour is, from vivid to greyish
How many different colours appear together in one design

quiz.q: A chart shows pass in green and fail in red with no labels or symbols. What is the best fix for colour-blind readers?
options: Make both colours more saturated so the difference between red and green is stronger
Use a green and a red of the same lightness so that neither colour looks stronger
Switch to orange and brown, which are easier to tell apart, and leave out any labels
Add labels or icons such as a tick and a cross, and keep a lightness difference

quiz.q: You need a logo that will be printed on a small badge and on a huge banner without becoming blurry. Which export is the best choice?
options: JPG
SVG
PNG at the smallest size
A screenshot of the logo

quiz.q: You are sending a photo-heavy flyer by WhatsApp to people with limited mobile data. Which export is usually most suitable?
options: JPG, because compression makes photos small
PNG, because it saves photos in the smallest file size
SVG, because photos are stored as vector shapes
PDF, because it compresses photos more than JPG does

quiz.q: Which of these is the correct reasoning about a 600 x 400 pixel photo being stretched to fill a full A4 page for printing at 300 ppi?
options: It will look sharp, because stretching a photo adds extra pixels and detail
It will look sharp, because JPG files keep their quality at any size
It will look blurry, because A4 at 300 ppi needs about 2480 x 3508 pixels
It will be blurry only when printed in colour, because black ink hides pixels

quiz.q: A designer uses six different fonts in one flyer so that it looks creative. What is the best advice?
options: Add even more fonts so that each line stands out more
Use only display fonts for all the text, including small print
Use all capital letters, with a different font for each line
Use one or two fonts, and vary size and weight for variety

quiz.q: A poster has a headline, details, and small print all in the same size and weight. What is the main problem?
options: There is too much white space, so the text looks too far apart
There is no visual hierarchy, so the eye does not know where to start
There is too much contrast, so the reader cannot see the words
The poster is too well aligned, so everything looks like a list

quiz.q: You found a lovely photo through an image search and want to use it on a paid advertisement. What should you do first?
options: Find the licence and check that it allows commercial use, or ask the owner
Use it, because pictures found on the internet are free to reuse in adverts
Use it and add the credit photo from Google underneath, which counts as permission
Use it after cropping it, because a changed image no longer needs permission

quiz.q: Which licence label means you must give credit and may not use the work for commercial purposes?
options: CC0
CC BY
Public domain
CC BY-NC

quiz.q: A designer wants a poster to be clear to a person standing at the far side of a school hall. What is the best choice for the headline?
options: Small, stylish text with thin letters in a light colour for elegance
Medium-sized text in pale grey on white, so it does not shout
Very large, bold text with strong contrast against the background
A long paragraph in a decorative font, so it explains the event fully

quiz.q: You test a design by converting it to greyscale and you can no longer tell two important sections apart. What does this suggest?
options: The design has too much white space, so the parts need to be filled
The fonts must all be serif, since greyscale hides sans serif text
The file must be exported as a PDF, because greyscale needs that format
The two parts differ only in hue, and need a difference in brightness

quiz.q: Which is true about margins and white space?
options: Empty space is wasted space, so a page looks better when it is filled
Empty space helps important items stand out and makes the design easier to read
Margins should differ on every side, so that the layout feels less rigid
White space is mainly useful on printed posters, and has little effect on phones

quiz.q: A club uses the same logo, the same two colours and the same font on every post, flyer and banner. Which CRAP principle does this show?
options: Contrast
Alignment
Repetition
Proximity
